questions.q: You drive a 40-foot truck at under 40 mph. What is the minimum following distance?
questions.a: 4 seconds
questions.e: Below 40 mph, leave at least one second for every 10 feet of vehicle length. 40 feet means 4 seconds.

questions.q: You drive a 40-foot truck at 55 mph. What is the minimum following distance?
questions.a: 5 seconds
questions.e: Above 40 mph, add one second to the one-second-per-10-feet rule. 4 seconds plus 1 equals 5.

questions.q: Total stopping distance is made up of which three parts?
questions.a: Perception distance, reaction distance and braking distance
w: Reaction distance, braking distance and coasting distance
Following distance, reaction distance and braking distance
Perception distance, steering distance and braking distance
questions.e: Total stopping distance is the distance you travel while you see the hazard, react to it and brake to a stop.

questions.q: About how long does it take an alert driver to react once they see a hazard?
questions.a: About three-quarters of a second
questions.e: The average alert driver takes about 3/4 of a second to react after seeing and recognizing a hazard.

questions.q: If you double your speed, your braking distance increases by about:
questions.a: Four times
questions.e: Braking distance grows with the square of speed. Double the speed and it takes roughly four times the distance to stop.

questions.q: Why does an empty truck often need more distance to stop than a loaded one?
questions.a: The brakes, tires and springs are designed for heavy loads, so an empty truck has less traction
w: Empty trucks have weaker brakes by law
It doesn't; empty trucks always stop shorter
questions.e: Brakes, tires, springs and shock absorbers work best when loaded. An empty truck can lock wheels and skid more easily.

questions.q: Hydroplaning can happen at speeds as low as:
questions.a: 30 mph
questions.e: With enough water on the road, tires can lose contact with the surface at speeds as low as 30 mph.

questions.q: How far ahead should you look while driving?
questions.a: 12 to 15 seconds ahead
questions.e: Looking 12 to 15 seconds ahead gives you time to spot hazards and change speed or lanes. At highway speed that is about a quarter mile.

questions.q: You stop on a two-lane road. Where do you place your rear warning triangle?
questions.a: About 100 feet behind the vehicle
questions.e: On a two-lane road, place one device within 10 feet of the vehicle on the traffic side, one about 100 feet behind and one about 100 feet ahead.

questions.q: You stop on a one-way or divided highway. Where do the warning devices go?
questions.a: 10 feet, 100 feet and 200 feet behind the vehicle
w: 10 feet behind, 100 feet behind and 100 feet ahead
50 feet, 100 feet and 150 feet behind the vehicle
All three directly behind the bumper
questions.e: Traffic only approaches from behind on a divided or one-way road, so all three devices go behind: at 10, 100 and 200 feet.

questions.q: You stop just past a hill or curve. How far back can the rear warning device go?
questions.a: Up to 500 feet
questions.e: If a hill, curve or other obstruction blocks the view, move the rear device back as far as 500 feet so drivers get enough warning.

questions.q: What is the minimum tread depth for steering axle tires?
questions.a: 4/32 inch
questions.e: Front (steering) tires need at least 4/32 inch of tread in every major groove. Other tires need at least 2/32 inch.

questions.q: Steering wheel free play is too much if it is more than about:
questions.a: 10 degrees (about 2 inches on a 20-inch wheel)
questions.e: More than 10 degrees of play, roughly 2 inches of movement at the rim of a 20-inch wheel, makes the vehicle hard to steer.

questions.q: During a pre-trip inspection, how many missing leaves in a leaf spring put the vehicle out of service?
questions.a: One-fourth or more of the leaves
w: Only if every leaf is missing
questions.e: A leaf spring with one-fourth or more of its leaves missing puts the vehicle out of service.

questions.q: What is the most common cause of serious skids?
questions.a: Driving too fast for conditions
questions.e: Most serious skids come from going too fast for road conditions. Over-braking, over-steering and over-accelerating also cause skids.

questions.q: Your drive wheels start to skid. What should you do first?
questions.a: Take your foot off the accelerator and stop braking
w: Accelerate to pull out of the skid
Turn the wheel away from the skid
questions.e: To regain traction, let the rear wheels roll again: stop braking, ease off the accelerator, then steer where you want to go and be ready to countersteer.

questions.q: In an emergency, why is steering away from a hazard often better than stopping?
questions.a: You can usually turn to miss an obstacle more quickly than you can stop
w: Brakes are not allowed in emergencies
questions.e: Top-heavy trucks need a lot of distance to stop. A quick turn often avoids the hazard in less space.

questions.q: If you must leave the road to avoid a crash, you should:
questions.a: Avoid braking until speed drops to about 20 mph, and keep one set of wheels on the pavement if you can
w: Brake as hard as possible right away
Turn sharply back onto the road at full speed
questions.e: Hard braking on a soft shoulder can cause a skid. Slow down gradually and keep one side on the pavement if possible.

questions.q: Your safe speed downhill is 40 mph. Using snub braking, when do you apply the brakes?
questions.a: At 45 mph, braking down to 35 mph
w: At 40 mph, braking down to 30 mph
At 50 mph, braking down to 40 mph
Hold the brakes lightly the whole way down
questions.e: When you reach 5 mph over your safe speed, brake firmly until you are 5 mph under it, then release. Repeat as needed.

questions.q: When should you choose a low gear for a long downgrade?
questions.a: Before you start down the grade
w: When the brakes start to fade
At the bottom of the grade
questions.e: Shifting down on a steep grade can be hard or impossible. Pick the right low gear before you start down.

questions.q: What is the legal blood alcohol limit for a CMV driver?
questions.e: Federal law sets the limit for commercial drivers at 0.04% blood alcohol concentration, half the usual limit for car drivers.

questions.q: Which fire extinguisher class is used on electrical fires?
questions.a: Class C
questions.e: Class C is for electrical fires. Class B is for flammable liquids like gasoline and grease. Most trucks carry a B:C extinguisher.

questions.q: When should you never remove the radiator cap?
questions.a: When the engine is hot
w: When checking the coolant at a truck stop
questions.e: The cooling system is under pressure when hot. Opening it can spray scalding coolant. Let the engine cool first.

questions.q: What is the minimum number of tiedowns for any flatbed load?
questions.a: Two, with at least one for every 10 feet of cargo
w: One for every 20 feet of cargo
One, as long as it is tight
questions.e: You need at least one tiedown per 10 feet of cargo and never fewer than two, no matter how small the load.

questions.q: After you start a trip, when must you first check your cargo and its securement?
questions.a: Within the first 50 miles
w: Only at the end of the day
questions.e: Check cargo within the first 50 miles, then every 3 hours or 150 miles, whichever comes first, and after every break.

questions.q: Objects in a convex (curved) mirror look:
questions.a: Smaller and farther away than they really are
w: Larger and closer than they really are
questions.e: Convex mirrors show a wider area but make things look smaller and farther away. Keep that in mind when judging distance.

questions.q: At night, you should switch to low beams when an oncoming vehicle is within:
questions.a: 500 feet
questions.e: Dim your lights within 500 feet of an oncoming vehicle and when following another vehicle so you don't blind the driver.

questions.q: When crossing railroad tracks, you should never:
questions.a: Shift gears while on the tracks
w: Roll down your window to listen
questions.e: Pick a gear that gets you all the way across before you start. Shifting on the tracks can stall the vehicle.

questions.q: When making a right turn, you should:
questions.a: Go straight ahead until the rear clears the curb, then turn, keeping the rear close to the curb
w: Swing wide to the left before turning
Turn as sharply as possible from the left lane
Use the shoulder to make the turn
questions.e: Swinging left before a right turn invites cars to pass you on the right. Keep the back of the trailer near the curb so no one can squeeze in.

questions.q: When backing, it is safest to back toward:
questions.a: The driver's side
w: Whichever way the trailer is already pointed
questions.e: Backing toward the driver's side lets you watch the rear of the vehicle by looking out the window. Use a helper whenever you can.

tests.name: Air Brakes
tests.who: Needed to drive any vehicle with air brakes, which covers most trucks and buses.

questions.q: At about what pressure does the governor stop the air compressor from pumping (cut-out)?
questions.a: 125 psi
questions.e: The governor stops the compressor at about 125 psi. It starts pumping again (cut-in) around 100 psi.

questions.q: At about what pressure does the governor let the compressor start pumping again (cut-in)?
questions.a: 100 psi
questions.e: Cut-in is about 100 psi. If it is much lower or higher than spec, the governor needs service.

questions.q: The low air pressure warning must come on before pressure in the tanks drops below:
questions.a: 60 psi
questions.e: The warning light, buzzer or wig wag must activate before supply pressure falls below 60 psi.

questions.q: In most vehicles, spring brakes come on automatically when air pressure drops to:
questions.a: Between 20 and 45 psi
questions.e: Spring brakes are held off by air. When pressure drops into the 20-45 psi range, the springs apply the brakes.

questions.q: With the engine off and brakes released, a single vehicle should lose no more than:
questions.a: 2 psi in one minute
questions.e: The static leakage limit is 2 psi per minute for a single vehicle and 3 psi per minute for a combination.

questions.q: With the engine off and the brake pedal held down, a single vehicle should lose no more than:
questions.a: 3 psi in one minute
questions.e: Applied leakage should stay under 3 psi per minute for a single vehicle and 4 psi per minute for a combination.

questions.q: In a dual air system, how long should it take to build pressure from 85 to 100 psi at fast idle?
questions.a: Within 45 seconds
questions.e: Build-up from 85 to 100 psi should take 45 seconds or less in a dual air system. Slower means a compressor or leak problem.

questions.q: At what pressure does the safety relief valve usually open?
questions.a: 150 psi
questions.e: The safety valve protects the tanks from too much pressure. It is usually set to open at 150 psi.

questions.q: Why are air tanks drained?
questions.a: To remove water and compressor oil that collect in them
w: To lower the pressure before driving
questions.e: Water and oil in the tanks can freeze or damage the system. Tanks without automatic drains should be drained at the end of each day.

questions.q: What is the most common type of foundation brake on air-brake trucks?
questions.a: S-cam drum brakes
questions.e: S-cam brakes are the most common. The S-shaped cam spreads the brake shoes against the drum.

questions.q: With the parking brake released and the engine off, how far should a manual slack adjuster move when pulled by hand?
questions.a: No more than about 1 inch where the pushrod attaches
w: It should not move at all under any condition
questions.e: If the slack adjuster moves more than about an inch, the brakes likely need adjusting.

questions.q: Brake drum cracks are a defect if they are:
questions.a: Longer than half the width of the friction area
w: Longer than the full width of the drum
Only if you can see daylight through them
questions.e: Drums must not have cracks longer than half the width of the friction area.

questions.q: Why does an air brake system take longer to stop than hydraulic brakes?
questions.a: Air takes time to flow through the lines to the brakes (brake lag)
w: Air brakes only work on the rear axles
Air brakes require you to pump the pedal
questions.e: Brake lag is about half a second. At 55 mph that adds roughly 32 feet to your stopping distance.

questions.q: What color and shape is the parking brake control knob?
questions.a: Yellow and diamond-shaped
questions.e: The parking brake control is a yellow diamond knob. The red eight-sided knob is the trailer air supply on combinations.

questions.q: When should you avoid using the parking brakes?
questions.a: When the brakes are very hot or very cold and wet
w: Any time the truck is parked
When the air pressure is above 100 psi
questions.e: Hot drums can be damaged when parking brakes apply, and wet brakes can freeze to the drums in cold weather. Use wheel chocks instead.

questions.q: What is an alcohol evaporator for?
questions.a: To reduce the risk of ice in brake valves and lines in cold weather
w: To clean oil from the tanks
To test a driver's blood alcohol
questions.e: It puts alcohol into the air system so moisture is less likely to freeze and block the brakes.

questions.q: The low air pressure warning comes on while you are driving. What should you do?
questions.a: Stop and safely park as soon as possible
w: Keep driving to the next terminal
Pump the brake pedal to build pressure
questions.e: Low pressure means you could lose braking ability or the spring brakes could lock up. Stop safely while you still control where.

questions.q: In a dual air system, the primary system usually operates the brakes on:
questions.a: The rear axle or axles
questions.e: Usually the primary system runs the rear brakes and the secondary system runs the front brakes. Both may serve the trailer.

questions.q: How do you test that the spring brakes come on automatically?
questions.a: Fan off air by pumping the brake pedal until the parking brake knob pops out, around 20 to 45 psi
questions.e: Pumping the pedal drops pressure. The parking brake valve should pop out in the 20-45 psi range on most vehicles.

questions.q: Air-braked trucks and buses built on or after March 1, 1998 must have:
questions.a: Anti-lock brakes (ABS)
questions.e: Federal rules require ABS on air-braked trucks and buses built on or after March 1, 1998. Tractors needed it a year earlier.

tests.name: Combination Vehicles
tests.who: Required for a Class A CDL (tractor-trailers).

questions.q: What is the 'crack-the-whip' effect?
questions.a: Rearward amplification, where a quick steering move can tip over the trailer
w: When the trailer brakes lock before the tractor's
When the fifth wheel comes unlocked
When the driver over-revs the engine
questions.e: Sudden steering is amplified toward the back of a combination. The rear trailer can tip over even if the tractor stays upright.

questions.q: What color is the emergency (supply) air line glad hand?
questions.a: Red
questions.e: The emergency or supply line is red. The service line is blue.

questions.q: What color is the service air line glad hand?
questions.a: Blue
questions.e: The blue service line carries air controlled by the brake pedal or trailer hand brake to apply the trailer brakes.

questions.q: What does the trailer air supply control look like?
questions.a: A red, eight-sided knob
questions.e: Push the red eight-sided knob in to supply the trailer with air. Pull it out to shut off air and apply the trailer emergency brakes.

questions.q: What happens if the emergency line breaks or comes apart while driving?
questions.a: The trailer emergency brakes come on
w: Nothing happens until you press the pedal
questions.e: Loss of pressure in the emergency line causes the trailer's emergency (spring) brakes to apply.

questions.q: The tractor protection valve closes automatically when air pressure drops to:
questions.a: Between 20 and 45 psi
questions.e: The valve keeps air in the tractor if the trailer lines break or leak badly. It closes in the 20-45 psi range.

questions.q: Should you use the trailer hand valve (trolley valve) to park?
questions.a: No, use the parking brakes
w: Yes, it holds better than parking brakes
questions.e: The hand valve uses service air, which can leak off and let the trailer roll. Always park with the spring parking brakes.

questions.q: When coupling, how high should the trailer be compared to the fifth wheel?
questions.a: Just low enough that the trailer is raised slightly when the tractor backs under it
w: Several inches above the fifth wheel
Exactly level with the top of the frame
As low as the landing gear will go
questions.e: If the trailer is too high it may not couple right. Set it so the fifth wheel lifts it slightly as you back under.

questions.q: After coupling, what should you see when you look at the fifth wheel?
questions.a: No space between the upper and lower fifth wheel, and the jaws locked around the shank of the kingpin
w: A small gap so the trailer can pivot
The jaws locked around the head of the kingpin
questions.e: A gap means the trailer is riding on the jaws or is high-coupled. The jaws must close around the kingpin shank, not the head.

questions.q: How do you test that the coupling is secure?
questions.a: With the trailer brakes locked, pull forward gently in low gear (a tug test)
w: Drive forward at speed and brake hard
Check that the air lines are connected
questions.e: A gentle tug against the locked trailer brakes confirms the kingpin is locked in the fifth wheel.

questions.q: Before driving away after coupling, the landing gear should be:
questions.a: Fully raised, with the crank handle secured
questions.e: Landing gear left partly down can catch on railroad tracks or other objects.

questions.q: During a turn, the trailer wheels follow a path that is:
questions.a: Shorter than the tractor wheels' path (off-tracking)
w: The same as the tractor wheels
questions.e: Off-tracking means the rear wheels cut inside the path of the front wheels, which is why you need to turn wide.

questions.q: Your trailer starts to swing out in a jackknife skid. What should you do?
questions.a: Release the brakes to let the wheels grip again
w: Use the trailer hand brake to straighten it
questions.e: Trailer jackknifes usually come from locked trailer wheels. Releasing the brakes lets the tires regain traction.

questions.q: Compared to an empty rig, a fully loaded rig is about how much more likely to roll over in a crash?
questions.a: About 10 times more likely
questions.e: The high center of gravity of a loaded trailer makes rollovers far more likely. Steer gently and take curves slowly.

questions.q: Which statement about combination vehicles and rollovers is true?
questions.a: Keeping cargo low and steering gently reduces rollover risk
w: Heavier loads should go on top
Rollovers only happen at highway speed
Rollovers only happen to empty trailers
questions.e: Keep the load as close to the ground as possible and avoid quick lane changes or tight turns at speed.

tests.name: Hazardous Materials
tests.who: For the H endorsement. Also requires a TSA background check.

questions.q: Where must placards appear on a vehicle that requires them?
questions.a: On all four sides
w: On the front and back only
questions.e: Placards must be on the front, rear and both sides, readable from each direction.

questions.q: Where must hazmat shipping papers be while you drive?
questions.a: In a pouch on the driver's door, or in clear view within reach while you wear your seat belt
w: In the trailer with the cargo
questions.e: Papers must be easy to reach for you or emergency responders. When you leave the cab, put them on the driver's seat or in the door pouch.

questions.q: Which hazard class covers flammable liquids such as gasoline?
questions.a: Class 3
questions.e: Class 3 is flammable liquids. Class 1 is explosives, Class 5 is oxidizers and Class 8 is corrosives.

questions.q: Which hazard class covers explosives?
questions.a: Class 1
questions.e: Class 1 is explosives, divided into divisions 1.1 through 1.6.

questions.q: Which hazard class covers corrosive materials?
questions.a: Class 8
questions.e: Class 8 is corrosives, like many acids. Class 6 is poisons and Class 7 is radioactive materials.

questions.q: How far from a vehicle loaded with explosives, flammables or oxidizers must you be to smoke?
questions.a: At least 25 feet
questions.e: No smoking or open flame within 25 feet of a vehicle carrying Class 1, Division 2.1, Class 3, 4 or 5 materials.

questions.q: A placarded vehicle must stop how far from the nearest rail at a railroad crossing?
questions.a: Between 15 and 50 feet
questions.e: Stop no closer than 15 feet and no farther than 50 feet, look and listen, then cross without shifting gears.

questions.q: A vehicle with Division 1.1, 1.2 or 1.3 explosives may not park within how far of a bridge, tunnel or building?
questions.a: 300 feet
questions.e: Do not park within 300 feet of a bridge, tunnel, building, open fire or place where people gather, and not within 5 feet of the road.

questions.q: On a placarded vehicle with dual tires, how often must you check the tires?
questions.a: At the start of each trip and each time you park
w: Only at the start of the trip
questions.e: Check tires at the start of every trip and every time you park. A hot or flat tire must be fixed before moving on.

questions.q: What does 'RQ' on a shipping paper mean?
questions.a: Reportable Quantity
questions.e: RQ means the material is a hazardous substance in an amount that must be reported to authorities if it spills.

questions.q: What book helps emergency responders identify hazardous materials by ID number?
questions.a: The Emergency Response Guidebook (ERG)
questions.e: The ERG lists actions to take for each material by its four-digit identification number.

questions.q: An identification number on a shipping paper or placard has how many digits?
questions.a: Four
questions.e: Hazmat ID numbers are four digits, preceded by UN or NA, such as UN1203 for gasoline.

questions.q: For Table 2 materials, placards are required once the total weight reaches:
questions.a: 1,001 pounds or more
questions.e: Table 1 materials need placards in any amount. Table 2 materials need them at 1,001 pounds or more aggregate gross weight.

questions.q: A placarded vehicle must carry a fire extinguisher with a UL rating of at least:
questions.a: 10 B:C
questions.e: The power unit of a placarded vehicle needs an extinguisher rated 10 B:C or more.

questions.q: A cargo tank that has been emptied but not cleaned or purged:
questions.a: Must still be placarded
questions.e: Residue can still be dangerous. Placards stay on until the tank has been cleaned or purged.

tests.name: Tank Vehicles
tests.who: For the N endorsement, needed to haul liquids or gases in bulk.

questions.q: When is a tank endorsement required?
questions.a: When hauling liquid or gas in a tank of 119 gallons or more, or tanks totaling 1,000 gallons or more
w: Any time the truck has a fuel tank
questions.e: The N endorsement is required for individual tanks of 119+ gallons or a total of 1,000+ gallons that are permanently or temporarily attached.

questions.q: What is liquid surge?
questions.a: Movement of liquid in a partly filled tank that pushes the truck in the direction the liquid moves
w: Rising pressure in the tank on hot days
questions.e: Surge can push a stopped truck forward into an intersection or make it hard to control on slippery roads.

questions.q: What do baffles inside a tank control?
questions.a: Front-to-back surge, but not side-to-side surge
questions.e: Baffles slow front-to-back liquid movement. Side-to-side surge still happens and can cause a rollover.

questions.q: Why are smooth-bore tanks especially hard to drive?
questions.a: They have no baffles, so front-to-back surge is very strong
w: They have no brakes on the trailer
questions.e: Smooth-bore tanks, often used for food products like milk, let liquid surge freely. Brake gently and allow extra distance.

questions.q: What is outage?
questions.a: Room left in a tank for the liquid to expand
w: The amount of liquid that leaked out
A tank that is out of service
The time a tank sits empty
questions.e: Liquids expand as they warm up. Never fill a tank completely; leave outage for expansion.

questions.q: Why are bulkheads used in tanks?
questions.a: To divide the tank into compartments
questions.e: Bulkheads split the tank into separate compartments. Watch weight distribution when loading and unloading them.

questions.q: Why do tankers have a high risk of rollover?
questions.a: They have a high center of gravity and the load can shift
w: Tankers are lighter than other trucks
questions.e: Most of the weight sits high off the road, and moving liquid can shift that weight suddenly in curves.

questions.q: How should you handle curves in a tank vehicle?
questions.a: Slow down before the curve, then accelerate slightly through it
w: Brake in the middle of the curve
Take the curve at the posted speed
questions.e: Braking in a curve adds to surge and rollover risk. Slow down before you enter and keep steady power through.

questions.q: When coming to a stop in a tanker, you should:
questions.a: Keep steady brake pressure and avoid releasing the brakes too soon
w: Release the brakes just before stopping
questions.e: Releasing too early lets surge push the truck forward. Brake smoothly and early, with steady pressure.

questions.q: Which load is generally the hardest to control because of surge?
questions.a: A partly filled tank
questions.e: A partial load has room for the liquid to move. That moving weight is what makes surge dangerous.

tests.name: Doubles and Triples
tests.who: For the T endorsement, needed to pull two or three trailers.

questions.q: Which trailer in a set of triples is most likely to turn over?
questions.a: The last trailer
questions.e: Rearward amplification, the crack-the-whip effect, is strongest at the back of the combination.

questions.q: Where should the heaviest trailer go in a set of doubles?
questions.a: Directly behind the tractor
questions.e: Put the heavier trailer up front. A heavy rear trailer increases the risk of sway and rollover.

questions.q: What is a converter dolly?
questions.a: A coupling device with one or two axles and a fifth wheel used to connect a second trailer
w: A device that converts air brakes to hydraulic
A jack used to raise the landing gear
questions.e: The converter dolly turns a semi-trailer into a full trailer so it can be pulled behind another trailer.

questions.q: Before coupling the second trailer, how do you keep it from moving?
questions.a: Make sure its spring brakes are set or chock the wheels
w: Leave it unsecured so it lines up easily
questions.e: If the second trailer doesn't have spring brakes, charge its air tanks and disconnect the emergency line to set its brakes, or chock it.

questions.q: After coupling doubles, how should the shut-off valves be set?
questions.a: Open on the first trailer, closed at the rear of the last trailer
w: Closed on the first trailer, open at the rear
questions.e: Open valves let air flow through to every trailer. The valves at the very rear must be closed so air doesn't escape.

questions.q: How can you check that air is flowing to all trailers?
questions.a: Open the emergency line shut-off valve at the back of the last trailer and listen for air escaping
w: Look at the glad hand colors
questions.e: Air rushing out of the rear valve shows the whole system is charged. Close the valve again before driving.

questions.q: Compared to a single trailer, doubles and triples need:
questions.a: More following distance and more space to change lanes
questions.e: Longer combinations take more distance to stop and are less stable. Leave more room in every direction.

questions.q: What usually connects the converter dolly to the trailer in front of it?
questions.a: A pintle hook
questions.e: The dolly's eye attaches to a pintle hook at the back of the trailer ahead.

questions.q: Why should steering be extra smooth when pulling doubles or triples?
questions.a: Sudden movements are amplified at the rear trailer and can cause rollovers
questions.e: A quick lane change that feels minor in the tractor can whip the last trailer hard enough to flip it.

questions.q: When pulling doubles, you should check that the converter dolly air tank is:
questions.a: Drained of moisture and its petcock closed before driving
questions.e: Drain moisture from the dolly tank, then close the petcock so the dolly brakes can work.

tests.name: Passenger Vehicles
tests.who: For the P endorsement, needed to drive buses with 16 or more people including the driver.

questions.q: How much allowed hazardous material may a bus carry in total?
questions.a: No more than 500 pounds
w: Any amount if it is labeled
questions.e: Buses may carry limited amounts of allowed hazmat: no more than 500 pounds total and no more than 100 pounds of any one class.

questions.q: Which of these is never allowed on a bus?
questions.a: Division 2.3 poison gas
w: A labeled container of oxygen for a passenger
A small amount of an allowed material properly packaged
questions.e: Division 2.3 poison gas, liquid Class 6 poisons, tear gas and irritating materials are forbidden on buses.

questions.q: What is the standee line?
questions.a: A line on the floor that passengers may not stand in front of
w: A line passengers wait behind at the bus stop
The line where the driver must stop at railroad crossings
questions.e: No rider may stand forward of the standee line while the bus is moving, because they would block the driver's view.

questions.q: At a railroad crossing, a bus must stop how far from the nearest rail?
questions.a: Between 15 and 50 feet
questions.e: Stop 15 to 50 feet from the tracks, open the forward door if it helps you see or hear, then cross without shifting gears.

questions.q: A bus must stop at least how far before a drawbridge without a signal light or attendant?
questions.a: 50 feet
questions.e: Stop at least 50 feet before the draw and look to make sure it is completely closed before crossing.

questions.q: Where should you discharge a disruptive passenger?
questions.a: At the next safe, well-lit stop
w: At the end of the route only
questions.e: Put them off at a safe, lighted place, like the next scheduled stop. Don't leave them in an unsafe spot.

questions.q: Can you refuel a bus with passengers on board?
questions.a: Not in a closed building with riders aboard
w: Yes, but only with the engine running
questions.e: Never refuel in a closed building with passengers on board, and avoid refueling with riders aboard whenever you can.

questions.q: Before driving, emergency exits on a bus should be:
questions.a: Checked and closed, with the handles working
w: Locked so passengers can't open them
Blocked by luggage so they don't rattle
questions.e: Emergency exits must be closed while driving but able to open, and never blocked.

questions.q: What should you never use in place of the parking brake on a transit bus?
questions.a: The brake-door interlock
questions.e: The interlock holds the bus while the rear door is open, but it releases when the door closes. Always set the parking brake.

questions.q: Where should baggage and freight be stored on a bus?
questions.a: Secured so the driver and passengers can move freely and exits aren't blocked
w: In the aisle so it's easy to reach
In front of the standee line
On empty seats near the emergency exit
questions.e: Aisles and exits must stay clear, and loose items can fly forward in a sudden stop.

tests.name: School Bus
tests.who: For the S endorsement, needed to drive a school bus. You'll also need the Passenger (P) endorsement.

questions.q: How far out from the bus does the danger zone extend?
questions.a: Up to 30 feet on all sides
w: Up to 5 feet on all sides
Up to 10 feet in front only
Up to 100 feet behind the bus
questions.e: The danger zone is the area on all sides of the bus where children are at greatest risk of being hit, by the bus or by passing traffic. It can extend up to 30 feet.

questions.q: Outside flat side mirrors should be adjusted so you can see about how far behind the bus?
questions.a: About 200 feet, or 4 bus lengths
questions.e: Set the flat mirrors so you can see about 200 feet (4 bus lengths) behind the bus along the sides.

questions.q: What are the crossover mirrors used for?
questions.a: Seeing the area directly in front of the bus and along the sides that you can't see from the seat
w: Seeing traffic far behind the bus
questions.e: Crossover mirrors show the blind area right in front of the bumper and the front of the bus, where small children can be hidden.

questions.q: What is the overhead inside mirror used for?
questions.a: Monitoring passenger activity inside the bus
w: Checking the area in front of the bus
questions.e: The inside overhead mirror lets you watch passengers without turning around.

questions.q: When approaching a stop, when should you turn on the alternating flashing amber lights?
questions.a: About 5 to 10 seconds before the stop, or as your state law requires
w: After the bus has fully stopped
Only if traffic is behind you
questions.e: The amber lights warn other drivers that you are about to stop. Turn them on early, usually about 5-10 seconds or 100-300 feet before the stop, depending on state law.

questions.q: When are the alternating flashing red lights used?
questions.a: When the bus is stopped to load or unload students
w: Any time the bus is moving in traffic
questions.e: Red lights and the stop arm tell traffic to stop while students get on or off.

questions.q: Students who must cross the road should walk how far in front of the bus?
questions.a: About 10 feet, where you can see them
w: Right up against the front bumper
questions.e: Students should cross about 10 feet in front of the bus so they stay in your direct line of sight.

questions.q: A student drops something near the bus. What should they do?
questions.a: Move away from the bus and ask the driver for help
w: Crawl under the bus to get it
Ask another student to grab it
questions.e: Bending down near the bus puts the student out of your sight. Tell students to never pick up dropped items and to come to you for help instead.

questions.q: Before pulling away from a stop, you should:
questions.a: Count the students and check all mirrors to make sure no one is near the bus
w: Wait for the students to wave
questions.e: Account for every student who got off. If you can't account for one, secure the bus and check around and under it.

questions.q: After an evacuation, students should go to a safe place at least how far from the road?
questions.a: 100 feet off the road, toward oncoming traffic
w: Across the road from the bus
questions.e: Moving toward oncoming traffic keeps students away from debris if another vehicle hits the bus.

questions.q: At a railroad crossing, a school bus should stop how far from the nearest rail?
questions.a: Between 15 and 50 feet
questions.e: Stop 15 to 50 feet from the tracks, then open the service door and your window and listen for a train.

questions.q: Before crossing railroad tracks, what should you do with the radio and other noisy equipment?
questions.a: Turn them off so you can hear a train
w: Turn the radio up to warn others
Turn on the heater fan to clear the windows
questions.e: Turn off radios and noisy equipment and ask students to be quiet so you can hear an approaching train.

questions.q: Your bus stalls on the railroad tracks. What should you do?
questions.a: Get everyone off right away and move them away from the tracks, toward the direction the train is coming from
w: Keep students seated and try to restart
Move students away in the same direction the train is going
Wait for the train to stop
questions.e: Evacuate immediately. Move students away from the tracks and toward the oncoming train so they aren't hit by debris after a collision.

questions.q: When a school bus turns, the rear can swing out up to:
questions.a: 3 feet
questions.e: Tail swing of up to 3 feet means the rear corner can hit people or objects next to the bus when turning. Check mirrors before and during turns.

questions.q: If you leave the driver's seat while students are on board, you should:
questions.a: Secure the bus: set the parking brake, put it in park or neutral, turn off the engine and remove the key
w: Leave the engine running so the heat stays on
Leave the key in for the next driver
questions.e: Never leave a bus with students aboard where it could be moved or rolled. Secure it completely first.
